notes: Complete Court of Appeal judgment on conviction and sentence appeals in Operation Kingsway heroin conspiracy.

enrichment.short_title: Conviction appeals dismissed and sentences largely upheld in Merseyside heroin conspiracy

statutes_considered.name: Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994

key_facts: Following a twelve-week trial at Liverpool Crown Court, multiple defendants were convicted of conspiracy to supply controlled drugs linked to Operation Kingsway, involving large-scale heroin importation via the Channel Tunnel between 1998 and 2000.
Lowe was sentenced to 24 years as a principal organiser; Parkinson to 21 years; several co-defendants received 16-year terms; Frederick, the disabled family-man courier, received 14 years.

Lowe appealed on grounds relating to exclusion of his defence statement from the jury and the judge's conspiracy direction; Parkinson and Davey challenged refusals to discharge the jury and identification directions.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) hearing appeals against conviction and sentence after single-judge leave decisions; Frederick's renewed conviction application had already been refused.
enrichment.outcome: Conviction appeals dismissed for Lowe, Parkinson and Davey; most sentence appeals dismissed; Jason Smith's sentence reduced from 16 to 13 years; Stephen Smith's reduced from 11 to 10 years.
enrichment.ratio: An extensive defence statement served months after interview is inadmissible as a previous consistent statement and does not undermine a proper section 34 direction; in conspiracy trials the jury decides participation in the agreement, not each defendant's relative role; jury discharge and Turnbull identification rulings are matters for the trial judge's discretion if properly directed; long sentences for senior participants in massive Class A drug conspiracies may be appropriate even where total importation cannot be precisely quantified.
legal_issues: Whether the trial judge erred in refusing to put Lowe's CPIA defence statement before the jury
Whether the conspiracy direction and response to the jury's question misdirected on Lowe's role
Whether cumulative prejudice required discharge of the jury in Parkinson's and Davey's trials
Whether identification and summing-up directions were adequate
Whether sentences of up to 24 years were manifestly excessive for organisers of a large heroin conspiracy

notes: Complete administrative court judgment on Immigration and Asylum Appeals (Procedure) Rules 2000.

enrichment.short_title: Faxed leave-to-appeal application not received where IAT clerk did not log it
key_facts: Mr Kamau, a Kenyan asylum seeker who entered the UK in December 1999, lost his asylum appeal before an adjudicator in May 2001; removal directions were later set.

His solicitors faxed an application for permission to appeal to the IAT on 19 June 2001 within the ten-day limit, but the tribunal had no record of receiving it; the file was not chased for nearly two years.
On detention in May 2003 he sought judicial review contending an outstanding permission application made subsequent removal unlawful.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Secretary of State's refusal to withdraw removal directions, following an out-of-hours stay granted by Blackburne J.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; no outstanding application for permission to appeal found; lottery order for costs.
enrichment.ratio: Under rule 48(4)-(5) of the 2000 Rules, a faxed notice of appeal is received by the appellate authority only when it arrives on the fax machine and is received by a clerk; absent evidence of receipt by a clerk, no application is outstanding even if the fax transmission report shows dispatch, and experienced solicitors are expected to chase non-acknowledged applications rather than allow years to pass.
legal_issues: Whether a faxed application for leave to appeal was validly received by the IAT
Whether removal directions were unlawful while a permission application was allegedly pending
Construction of rules 18, 46 and 48 of the 2000 Procedure Rules
Whether strict construction of receipt rules works injustice in asylum cases

notes: Complete Court of Appeal judgment on corporate deed delivery and escrow; source summary truncated.

enrichment.short_title: Sealed council lease not delivered where completion awaited under subject-to-contract negotiations
key_facts: Bolton Council negotiated a 125-year lease of redevelopment land (Plots A and B) with Mr Torkington from 1985, correspondence being subject to contract; Torkington occupied and improved the land.
In September 1990 the Council sealed an engrossed lease in readiness for completion by 1 October but retained it; Torkington did not complete on time and later sought to enforce the lease.
After protracted dispute and possession proceedings from 1992, Lloyd J held there was no concluded lease; Torkington appealed on section 74(1) LPA 1925, delivery, escrow and quiet enjoyment grounds.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to Court of Appeal after refusal of permission below; Aldous LJ granted permission on escrow-related grounds.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed with costs; possession order upheld subject to conditional stay; permission to appeal to House of Lords refused.
enrichment.ratio: Section 74(1) of the Law of Property Act 1925 deems due execution by a corporation but does not dispense with the separate common law requirement of delivery; where negotiations are subject to contract, sealing a lease in anticipation of completion does not show intention to be bound immediately or as an escrow, and escrow conditions including payment were not fulfilled.
legal_issues: Whether section 74(1) LPA 1925 deems delivery as well as execution
Whether sealing by the Council imported delivery or a rebuttable presumption of delivery
Whether the lease was held in escrow and conditions were satisfied on 16 February 1991
Whether the Council breached covenant for quiet enjoyment or derogated from grant

notes: Complete case stated appeal on EU tachograph regulations; source summary truncated.

enrichment.short_title: Unladen tractor en route for export required working tachograph under EU regulations
key_facts: On 4 July 2002 Mr Field drove a 17-tonne tractor unit without trailer from Leighton Buzzard to Southampton docks for export to South Africa; no working tachograph or disc was fitted.
Southampton magistrates held the journey was outside Regulations 3820/85 and 3821/85 because the vehicle was unladen, on trade plates, and being exported.
VOSA appealed by case stated; the operator and driver were described as morally innocent test cases in tangled driver-hours legislation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from magistrates' acquittal to the Administrative Court.
enrichment.outcome: Magistrates' answer held wrong in law; case not remitted against Mr Field or the company in exercise of discretion; costs not awarded to defendants.
enrichment.ratio: Read purposively and as a whole, Regulations 3820/85 and 3821/85 require recording equipment in vehicles of types capable of carriage by road, subject to defined exemptions, regardless of the immediate purpose of a particular journey; an unladen tractor designed to pull trailers remains within scope even when driven to docks for export.
legal_issues: Meaning of 'used for the carriage of passengers or goods by road' in Article 3 of Regulation 3821/85
Whether construction/adaptation or actual use on the day determines tachograph obligation
Interaction of English strict construction of penal statutes with purposive EU construction
Appropriate disposal where defendants acted as test cases without moral blame

notes: Complete Chancery preliminary issue judgment on Millharbour boundary; source summary truncated.

enrichment.short_title: Docklands boundary fixed by measured Plan 4.70 favouring claimant's A-B line
key_facts: Hunt owned 45 Millharbour (Pritchard House); Weston Homes owned 41 Millharbour and controlled the owner of 43 Millharbour; plots were created by LDDC in the 1980s Docklands redevelopment.
In late 2001 Weston began redevelopment and erected hoarding and foundations; Hunt claimed encroachment of about 0.5 metres onto No. 45 along the northern boundary.
Competing boundary lines derived from inconsistent LDDC plans; Plan 4.70 (October 1985), signed by LDDC and PDX, precisely measured the southern boundary of Plot F6 along a gravel path.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Preliminary issue trial before Peter Smith J on whether the common boundary followed the claimant's or defendant's plan line.
enrichment.outcome: Boundary determined along line A-B on the Particulars of Claim plan; claimant's encroachment case on that line established at preliminary stage.
enrichment.ratio: Where title plans and Land Registry filed plans are imprecise general boundaries, a contemporaneous measured plan (Plan 4.70) fixing the southern boundary of No. 43 by site measurement and signed by the parties' predecessors is decisive; projecting that straight boundary northwards accords with the intended rectangular succession of LDDC plots and defeats the defendant's case requiring an interstitial strip.
legal_issues: Which plan correctly delineated the boundary between Nos 41/43 and 45 Millharbour
Weight to be given to Building Agreement Plan A dimensions versus later measured Plan 4.70
Whether Land Registry title plans assist boundary demarcation
Effect of hoarding and piling positions on boundary location

notes: Complete judicial review on HMRC decision not to assess AOL for VAT on ISP packages.

enrichment.short_title: HMRC lawfully declined VAT assessment of AOL pending EU e-commerce directive
key_facts: Freeserve, a UK ISP, sought judicial review of HMRC's March 2002 decision not to assess America Online for VAT on composite Internet service packages supplied to UK customers from June 2001.
AOL's packages combined telecoms access with content; under Card Protection Plan principles liability depended on whether telecoms services predominated.
HMRC concluded evidence was insufficient to sustain an assessment and that EU Directive 2002/38/EC would soon harmonise taxation of all electronic packages.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of Commissioners' decision evidenced by Treasury letter and Business Brief 06/2002.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; alleged errors of irrelevant considerations and excessive evidential threshold not established; court indicated Freeserve would lack standing even if errors were proved.
enrichment.ratio: When exercising section 73 VATA assessment discretion, HMRC may legitimately weigh the imminent arrival of EU legislation levelling VAT on all Internet packages; that is relevant to resource allocation and not Wednesbury irrational; contemporaneous ministerial correspondence does not displace detailed witness evidence of merits-based assessment, and phrases such as 'unambiguously predominated' in public briefs do not establish a universal evidential threshold for assessments.
legal_issues: Whether HMRC took an irrelevant consideration in relying on forthcoming EU VAT and e-commerce directive
Whether HMRC set too high a threshold before exercising section 73 assessment powers
Whether Freeserve had standing to challenge tax treatment of competitor AOL
Predominance of telecoms services in composite ISP packages under CPP principles

notes: Complete Commercial Court preliminary issue on SPA warranty notice requirements.

enrichment.short_title: Buyer precluded from antitrust warranty claim for non-compliant Schedule 8 notice
key_facts: Laminates acquired BTR's shareholding in FM Holdings/Formica Corporation under a March 1998 SPA for about US$415M with extensive Agreed Assurances in Schedule 7 and limitation provisions in Schedule 8.

From April 1999 Formica was subject to US Department of Justice Grand Jury antitrust investigation into HPL price-fixing; Laminates sent notices referencing Schedule 8 paragraph 3(A)(i) but not paragraph 2's formal claim requirements before 31 March 2000.
Private treble-damages antitrust class actions followed; Laminates sought to claim breach of paragraph 10(D) warranty that Formica was not party to prohibited competition arrangements.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Preliminary issue on reformulated question ordered by Cresswell J: whether failure to comply with Schedule 8 paragraph 2 bars the paragraph 10(D) claim.
enrichment.outcome: Preliminary issue answered in the affirmative; Laminates precluded from bringing the paragraph 10(D) warranty claim.
enrichment.ratio: Paragraph 2 of Schedule 8 requires a written notice actually asserting a claim against the vendor under the Agreed Assurances, specifying the matter giving rise to the claim, the nature of the claim and the amount claimed; notices framed only under paragraph 3(A)(i) as potential third-party matters 'may result in a claim' do not satisfy paragraph 2, and the buyer must give available detail—including alleged breach of warranty 10(D) and quantified or estimated loss—even where antitrust investigation details remain incomplete.
legal_issues: Distinction between paragraph 2 and paragraph 3(A)(i) notices under Schedule 8
Whether April 1999 and March 2000 correspondence satisfied paragraph 2 time limit
Required content of notice as to matter, nature and amount of warranty claim
Effect of buyer's limited knowledge during ongoing DOJ investigation

notes: Complete Divisional Court judgment on Terrorism Act 2000 section 44 stop and search at arms fair protest.

enrichment.short_title: Section 44 terrorism stop-and-search authorisation lawful at Docklands arms fair

statutes_considered.name: Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994

key_facts: Kevin Gillan (cyclist protester) and Pennie Quinton (journalist) were stopped and searched near the Excel Centre arms fair on 9 September 2003 under a metropolitan-wide section 44 authorisation confirmed by the Secretary of State.
Successive section 44(1) and (2) authorisations covering the whole Metropolitan Police district had been renewed every 28 days since February 2001 in response to substantial terrorism threat levels.
Claimants challenged the authorisation as ultra vires, police misuse against peaceful protestors, and ECHR proportionality; nothing incriminating was found.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Substantive judicial review after permission granted in consolidated applications raising sections 44(1) and 44(2) powers.
enrichment.outcome: All grounds rejected; authorisation and its use near the arms fair held lawful; private law remedies left open.
enrichment.ratio: Section 44 authorisation may cover an entire police area where a senior officer considers it expedient for prevention of terrorism and the Secretary of State confirms it; 'expedient' confers broad discretion subject to limited judicial review; police use near a high-risk symbolic target during substantial threat can be lawful even where protestors are stopped, provided powers are not exercised for reasons unconnected with terrorism, though PACE Code A guidance and Form 5090 require improvement.
legal_issues: Whether section 44 authorisation must be limited to imminent threats at specific locations
Whether stop/search of arms fair protestors was an improper use of counter-terrorism powers
Whether authorisation and searches were a proportionate interference with ECHR Articles 8, 9, 10 and 11
Construction of 'expedient' in section 44(3)

notes: Complete judicial review on Article 8 and Kosovo asylum removal; source summary truncated.

enrichment.short_title: Kosovo Albanian's Article 8 claim rejected on PTSD treatment availability
key_facts: Mr Ducja, born 1983 in Mitrovica, Kosovo, claimed asylum in July 2000 alleging January 2000 beating and house burning by Serbian security forces; Special Adjudicator found him Albanian not Roma.

Asylum and Article 3 claims failed on safe return and internal relocation; on remittal the Special Adjudicator considered Article 8 in light of PTSD for which he received outpatient treatment in the UK.
Secretary of State relied on IAT decision in Thaqi that adequate PTSD treatment existed in Kosovo; IAT refused leave to appeal citing inadequate proportionality analysis.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of Immigration Appeal Tribunal refusal of leave to appeal Special Adjudicator's Article 8 determination.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; Special Adjudicator's Article 8 reasoning held adequate; no need to remit for proportionality where Article 8(1) not engaged.
enrichment.ratio: Following Razgar guidance (applied retrospectively), a Special Adjudicator who compares UK psychiatric treatment with available PTSD treatment in Kosovo and concludes return would not cause sufficiently serious harm to physical and moral integrity has adequately addressed Article 8(1); where no prima facie breach is established, proportionality under Article 8(2) need not be considered; IAT criticism of failure to address proportionality was itself erroneous.
legal_issues: Whether Special Adjudicator adequately applied Article 8 territoriality and seriousness tests
Availability of PTSD treatment in Kosovo on return
Relationship between failed Article 3 claim and Article 8 claim
Whether IAT erred in refusing leave for lack of proportionality analysis

notes: Complete Court of Appeal judgment on Limitation Act section 33 discretion in occupational disease claim.

enrichment.short_title: Section 33 discretion exercised to allow late bladder cancer claim after third cluster case
key_facts: Mr Fletcher sued Containerbase for bladder cancer allegedly caused by hazardous chemical exposure while employed from 1977 to March 1984; cancer was diagnosed in 1990 but proceedings issued on 17 December 2002.
Judge Holman found date of knowledge in summer 1995, so limitation expired in summer 1998; permission to appeal the knowledge date was refused.
Learning of a third employee with bladder cancer and a statistical cluster report from Mr Clark in June 2002 gave Fletcher sufficient confidence to commence proceedings.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against exercise of section 33(3) discretion to disapply limitation; permission granted on point relating to third co-worker's unexpired claim, though that point was not pursued.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; section 33 discretion upheld; respondents' costs assessed at £8,585.14.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 33 the court may allow a late personal injury claim where the balance of prejudice favours the claimant; emergence of a third case of the same disease strengthening epidemiological evidence can shift a finely balanced discretion even though historic evidential difficulties for the defendant on precautions and instructions remain, especially where relevant documents were destroyed before the limitation period expired.
legal_issues: Whether the judge erred in treating a third employee's bladder cancer as the decisive section 33 factor
Prejudice to defendant from delay in proving workplace precautions and instructions
Whether discovery of cluster medical evidence changed the evidential landscape after limitation expired
Interaction of date of knowledge under section 14 and discretion under section 33
